title.narrative: Power of Pride Africa

description.narrative: Working towards diverse and inclusive societies in which LGBTI are able to participate to their full potential

"1. Individual LGBTI know and accept their SOGIESC and can ensure their rights in society are respected. They can meaningfully engage with societal structures. 2 A support system for LGBTI is developed based on discussions about common issues, needs and challenges, creating the motivation to act against discrimination and marginalisation. 3 LGBTI CBOs can strategically engage in societal and political decision-making processes using evidence-based advocacy. 4 Agile LGBTI movements are built that can work collectively to create social and political change and respond flexibly to various situations. 5 Institutions and other allies have an internal drive to include LGBTI in their decision-making and other structures. LGBTI are actively engaged in processes and all policy-making spaces. 6 Strong and reliable laws and policies are in place for LGBTI and are enforced by all relevant bodies. Follow-up on these policies and their implementation are under scrutiny "

comment.narrative: Baseline was produce in collaboration with partners in country. Consultants typically had virtual meetings with members of the participatory grant making mechanism, or representatives of partners in the country. During these meetings consultants reflected together with the partners on how best to collect the baseline data and considered the different options for who could undertake the research. In some countries it was agreed that partners would directly collect the data and in other cases partners confirmed the appointment of or co-selected a researcher. Consultants contracted with relevant organisations or individuals in each country and ensured that they were briefed about the process, provided the organisations with the baseline template as well as the tools that had been developed and how best to administer them. The research in each country then took different forms including a desktop review, which included integrating data from the Country Context Analyses (CCA)and other relevant documents, facilitating focus groups (some hybrid) as well as individual interviews and surveys with each of the partners to collect qualitative data and quantitative data. Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In total consultants received 162 partner responses and 1359 member responses to the surveys.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

Through the programme we have worked hard to provide information to LGBTI community members, contributing to more understanding and knowledge of individual coping strategies. In one of our country partners, for instance, partners hosted a series of community round tables to discuss empowerment, SRHR, (cyber)bullying, mental health challenges, legal awareness, and socio-economic empowerment. As a result, participants of the round tables have formed their own social networks to stay in contact via group chat. In three different countries we have contributed with the programme to improving the self-esteem and knowledge on SOGIESC of 50 LGBTI living with disabilities, 20 GBMSM and transwomen living with HIV and 20 GBMSM and 83 transgender people. In another country, a partner organisation empowered and inspired young queer women creatives with a storytelling contest that led to an online campaign for youth, bringing visibility to LGBTI narratives. Finally, despite the challenges of two of our most difficult contexts, partners decided to focus on what they could do for their communities and closed 2021 with a milestone each. In one of them, partners managed to create an online space that gathers resources, promotes awareness, and mitigates the isolation of individuals who lack a physical community. In the other one, partners decided to make psychosocial counselling available for 60 LBQT community members.

PAI (Organizationhas actively taken part in creating, convening, and supporting various initiatives aimed at advancing LGBTIQ+ rights and equality in Africa. They have undertaken several significant activities:
In terms of multilateral engagement, PAI organised a side event at the Africa Regional Forum on SD to raise awareness about the exclusion of LGBTIQ+ persons in the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Africa. This event specifically focused on SDGs 6, 7, 9, 11, and 17, which encompass water, energy, industry, cities, and partnerships.
Furthermore, PAI organised its 6th Regional Conference, providing a platform for activists from across the continent to participate in workshops, panels, and sessions that fostered awareness and capacity building. The conference facilitated connections between activists, donors, international organisations, and government officials, thereby strengthening networks within the African LGBTIQ+ movement.
Capacity strengthening has been a key focus for PAI. PAI conducted a training of trainers programme on human rights mechanisms, equipping activists with the necessary skills to engage in regional and international human rights mechanisms. These trained activists were then supported in conducting similar training programs in their respective countries or regions.
PAI also organised a leadership training programme for young LGBTIQ+ activists, aiming to enhance their leadership competencies within their communities or organisations. In Nigeria, PAI provided human rights mechanisms training to activists, enabling them to develop a stakeholder report for the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) process and receive coaching for the UPR advocacy week in Geneva.
To advocate for the inclusion of LGBTIQ+ rights in the implementation of the SDGs, PAI trained activists on utilising the SDGs accountability process. They supported activists' engagement in voluntary national reviews (VNR) and high-level political forum (HLPF) processes, ensuring their voices and concerns were heard.
PAI organized a leadership forum specifically tailored for Sexual and Gender Minority (SGM) women within the LGBTIQ+ movement. This forum aimed to build their leadership competencies and empower them to play pivotal roles in advancing the rights and equality of the SGM community.Lastly, PAI provided human rights mechanisms training to activists in Cameroon, equipping them with knowledge on how to effectively utilise the UN and Africa regional human rights mechanisms to address LGBTIQ+ rights violations and seek justice.
Through these various initiatives, PAI has worked tirelessly to raise awareness, build capacity, and advocate for the rights and equality of the LGBTIQ+ community in Africa.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

Partners carried out many different forms of advocacy on a national level, towards provincial governments, national ministries and societal actors, government institutions and societal actors. Whilst most partners engaged in advocacy regarding better access to services such as healthcare and education, mentioned under ‘mobilising allies’ – essential lobbying actions were undertaken in tow of our country partners, in direct response to the negative threats to the legal space. This included the fight against anti-LGBTI legislation and the involvment of UN agencies, as well as a Dutch embassy. Regional advocacy work took place at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the African Union (AU) and the Treaty Monitoring Body (TMB) at the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which is a part of the UN. In October/November 2021, PAI conducted a human rights and international advocacy training, for the countries who were up for review at the ACHPR at the time. 31 participants from 13 different countries were equipped with practical knowledge and training on how to effectively engage the ACHPR, as well as their own states and government. During this training, PAI facilitated the development of country-specific advocacy strategies, as well as the development of a collective regional strategic on SOGIESC. These strategies include engagements before, during and after the official review. ILGA Asia supported a young transgender activist in November 2021. This activist was able to join a mission in Geneva and engage with members of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. She held 5 meetings with the CERD committee members, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Federation for Human Rights members, and officials from the OHCHR in Geneva. Globally, there were many, many opportunities to engage in human rights and policy spaces. Due to the sheer number of these, Power of Pride prioritised the Human Rights Council (HRC), the Universal Periodic Reviews (UPRs) the UN High Level Political Forum (HLPF), the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

The training program conducted for Nigerian activists marked a significant milestone in their journey to advance LGBTIQ+ rights. With the support of a dedicated consultant, the activists collaboratively developed a comprehensive Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder report. This report, submitted to the Human Rights Council, served as a powerful tool to shed light on the human rights situation of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Nigeria and advocate for their rights on a global platform. The UPR training program not only empowered Nigerian activists with the technical expertise to navigate the UPR process but also fostered a sense of collaboration and unity among them. Working together to develop the stakeholder report and participate in advocacy efforts created a strong foundation for continued collaboration and advocacy in the future. Moving forward, PAI remains committed to supporting Nigerian activists as they analyze the outcomes of the UPR process and utilize its recommendations to influence their work for the next UPR cycle. This ongoing support will ensure that the voices and experiences of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Nigeria continue to be heard and that their rights are protected and promoted.

During the past year, Africa has witnessed a dynamic landscape of progress and challenges concerning legal and policy changes related to LGBTIQ+ rights. Notably, there was a significant milestone in Mauritius, where the Supreme Court made a groundbreaking judgement by decriminalising same-sex activities, marking a historic moment for equality and human rights. This progressive step forward demonstrated a growing recognition of the rights of LGBTIQ+ individuals in the region. The programme's continuous advocacy support was a major factor in the historic decision. Through sustained efforts, organisations and activists worked diligently to raise awareness, challenge discriminatory laws, and promote human rights for LGBTIQ+ individuals in Mauritius.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

description.narrative: This indicatior measures actions undertaken by grassroots organisations, CBOs and CSOs to reach out to LGBTI individuals and communities for the following purposes: provision of information on SOGIESC, human rights of LGBTI people, legal rights within national and regional frameworks, building self-esteem and integrating acceptance within LGBTI individuals and communities and enabling LGBTI individuals to engage with societal structures meaningfully.

comment.narrative: Baseline was produce in collaboration with partners in country. Consultants typically had virtual meetings with members of the participatory grant making mechanism, or representatives of partners in the country. During these meetings consultants reflected together with the partners on how best to collect the baseline data and considered the different options for who could undertake the research. In some countries it was agreed that partners would directly collect the data and in other cases partners confirmed the appointment of or co-selected a researcher. Consultants contracted with relevant organisations or individuals in each country and ensured that they were briefed about the process, provided the organisations with the baseline template as well as the tools that had been developed and how best to administer them. The research in each country then took different forms including a desktop review, which included integrating data from the Country Context Analyses (CCA)and other relevant documents, facilitating focus groups (some hybrid) as well as individual interviews and surveys with each of the partners to collect qualitative data and quantitative data. Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In total consultants received 162 partner responses and 1359 member responses to the surveys.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

Through the programme we have worked hard to provide information to LGBTI community members, contributing to more understanding and knowledge of individual coping strategies. In one of our country partners, for instance, partners hosted a series of community round tables to discuss empowerment, SRHR, (cyber)bullying, mental health challenges, legal awareness, and socio-economic empowerment. As a result, participants of the round tables have formed their own social networks to stay in contact via group chat. In three different countries we have contributed with the programme to improving the self-esteem and knowledge on SOGIESC of 50 LGBTI living with disabilities, 20 GBMSM and transwomen living with HIV and 20 GBMSM and 83 transgender people. In another country, a partner organisation empowered and inspired young queer women creatives with a storytelling contest that led to an online campaign for youth, bringing visibility to LGBTI narratives. Finally, despite the challenges of two of our most difficult contexts, partners decided to focus on what they could do for their communities and closed 2021 with a milestone each. In one of them, partners managed to create an online space that gathers resources, promotes awareness, and mitigates the isolation of individuals who lack a physical community. In the other one, partners decided to make psychosocial counselling available for 60 LBQT community members.

Partners carried out many different forms of advocacy on a national level, towards provincial governments, national ministries and societal actors, government institutions and societal actors. Whilst most partners engaged in advocacy regarding better access to services such as healthcare and education, mentioned under ‘mobilising allies’ – essential lobbying actions were undertaken in tow of our country partners, in direct response to the negative threats to the legal space. This included the fight against anti-LGBTI legislation and the involvment of UN agencies, as well as a Dutch embassy. Regional advocacy work took place at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the African Union (AU) and the Treaty Monitoring Body (TMB) at the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which is a part of the UN. In October/November 2021, PAI conducted a human rights and international advocacy training, for the countries who were up for review at the ACHPR at the time. 31 participants from 13 different countries were equipped with practical knowledge and training on how to effectively engage the ACHPR, as well as their own states and government. During this training, PAI facilitated the development of country-specific advocacy strategies, as well as the development of a collective regional strategic on SOGIESC. These strategies include engagements before, during and after the official review. ILGA Asia supported a young transgender activist in November 2021. This activist was able to join a mission in Geneva and engage with members of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. She held 5 meetings with the CERD committee members, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Federation for Human Rights members, and officials from the OHCHR in Geneva. Globally, there were many, many opportunities to engage in human rights and policy spaces. Due to the sheer number of these, Power of Pride prioritised the Human Rights Council (HRC), the Universal Periodic Reviews (UPRs) the UN High Level Political Forum (HLPF), the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).

During our diplomatic mission focused on the LGBTIQ+ situation in Africa, we successfully engaged with the Finnish Embassy, which provided us with a valuable platform to interact with the Minister of Justice. Our primary objective was to enhance their understanding of the current challenges faced by LGBTIQ+ individuals on the continent. With the assistance of our contact person at the Finnish Embassy, we were invited to meet with the Minister to discuss the importance of EU support and the support of the Finnish government in promoting human rights protection for LGBTIQ+ people. This was instrumental in raising awareness about the urgent need to address the issues faced by LGBTIQ+ individuals in Africa. We shared comprehensive information on the prevailing situation, emphasising the importance of concerted efforts to advance the rights and equality of LGBTIQ+ individuals. Furthermore, we highlighted the significance of EU support and collaboration with the Finnish government to drive positive change.We will continue to foster our partnership with the Finnish Embassy.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

The training program conducted for Nigerian activists marked a significant milestone in their journey to advance LGBTIQ+ rights. With the support of a dedicated consultant, the activists collaboratively developed a comprehensive Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder report. This report, submitted to the Human Rights Council, served as a powerful tool to shed light on the human rights situation of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Nigeria and advocate for their rights on a global platform.
The training provided an invaluable opportunity for an activist to receive specialised coaching and participate in the UPR advocacy week in Geneva. This immersive experience equipped the activist with the necessary skills and knowledge to effectively engage with stakeholders, policymakers, and human rights experts at the international level. The UPR training programme not only empowered Nigerian activists with the technical expertise to navigate the UPR process but also fostered a sense of collaboration and unity among them. Working together to develop the stakeholder report and participate in advocacy efforts created a strong foundation for continued collaboration and advocacy in the future.PAI remains committed to supporting Nigerian activists as they analyse the outcomes of the UPR process and utilise its recommendations to influence their work for the next UPR cycle. This ongoing support will ensure that the voices and experiences of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Nigeria continue to be heard and that their rights are protected and promoted.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

PAI formed a crucial partnership with the African Civil Society Engagement platform, which includes organizations like Amnesty International, ISLA, Synergia for Human Rights, MOLI, and others. This collaboration greatly supported PAI's work at the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR).
The partnership involved capacity-building initiatives, where activists were equipped with the necessary skills to engage effectively with the African Commission. The coalition members provided expertise and resources to empower activists in navigating the Commission's mechanisms and procedures.
Furthermore, the partnership facilitated direct interactions between activists and Commissioners at the African Commission. Through the coalition's support, activists had opportunities to engage with Commissioners, share their experiences, and advocate for the rights of LGBTIQ+ individuals.
In addition, PAI, together with Amnesty International and other partners, made a joint statement at the 77th session of the ACHPR. This collective effort utilized the platform of the African Commission to raise awareness about the challenges faced by the LGBTIQ+ community and emphasize the need for inclusive policies, legal protection, and social acceptance.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

In its pursuit of advancing LGBTIQ+ rights in Africa, PAI has been actively engaged in various diplomatic, advocacy, and capacity-building initiatives. One notable achievement was PAI's diplomatic engagement with the Finnish Embassy, where they advocated for EU and Finnish government support in protecting the human rights of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Africa. This collaboration aimed to foster equality and rights for the LGBTIQ+ community by garnering international support.
PAI has also focused on raising awareness about the inclusion of LGBTIQ+ individuals in the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Africa. Through discussions and presentations, participants gained insights into the existing gaps and challenges faced by the community in accessing and benefiting from SDG programs in sectors like water, energy, industries, cities, and partnerships. This increased awareness will help drive future efforts to ensure the rights and well-being of LGBTIQ+ individuals are considered in SDG implementation.
The organization's involvement in the 67th Session of the Commission on the Status of Women (CSW) provided valuable insights on effectively engaging LBQTI women at the UN. PAI's Advocacy Manager gained knowledge and perspectives from diplomats, international organizations, and fellow activists, which will inform strategies to facilitate LBQTI persons' engagement at the CSW and advocate for their rights.
To better understand the situation of LGBTIQ+ individuals in East Africa, PAI organized the Changing Faces Changing Spaces Conference, creating a platform for activists and stakeholders to share their experiences and challenges. This firsthand information will inform future support initiatives aimed at advancing the rights of the LGBTIQ+ community in the region.
